props.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
props.initialSlug: A town's myth hides the truth of a famous killing

sections.content: John Ford's **The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance** (1962) represents a pivotal moment in Western cinema, deliberately deconstructing the myths of the American West. Shot in stark black and white when color westerns were standard, Ford pairs James Stewart and John Wayne to explore the tension between civilization and frontier justice. The film's famous line "When the legend becomes fact, print the legend" cuts to the heart of how the West was romanticized, connecting directly to earlier mythmaking westerns like **My Darling Clementine** (1946) and **Stagecoach** (1939).

sections.content: The film's layered examination of violence and progress found new resonance in later revisionist Westerns. **McCabe & Mrs. Miller** (1971) picked up similar themes of civilization's advance, while **The Wild Bunch** (1969) violently portrayed the death of the Old West. But Liberty Valance's sophisticated handling of truth versus myth influenced everything from **Once Upon a Time in the West** (1968) to **The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford** (2007).

The central dynamic between Stewart's idealistic lawyer and Wayne's pragmatic gunman established a template for exploring the costs of progress. This complexity influenced neo-westerns like **No Country for Old Men** (2007) and **Hell or High Water** (2016), which similarly examine how violence and justice intersect with changing times. The film's structure, using flashback to contrast myth with reality, became a crucial technique for deconstructing western legends. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

movies.title: Rio Bravo
movies.slug: Howard Hawks' response to High Noon, featuring John Wayne as a sheriff who refuses to face danger alone

sections.content: Beyond westerns, Liberty Valance's exploration of truth versus legend resonates in films like **The Last Duel** (2021) and **Rashomon** (1950), which similarly question historical narrative and perspective. The film's sophisticated handling of political themes - the transition from frontier law to democratic governance - influenced later political dramas like **All the President's Men** (1976) and **Lincoln** (2012).
